lawyer:
Mr. Md. Raziur Rahman Chowdhury, Advocate ------ for the appellant
Syed Abu Kowser, A.A.G ------ for the State
parties:
Abdul Qaium ------ Appellant
Vs.
The State ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
7. The learned Sessions Judge Narsingdi on consideration of the evidence on record as well as facts and circumstances of the case found the accused-appellant guilty of the offence charged and accordingly convicted him under section 302/34 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to suffer imprisonment for life and to pay fine with default clause as mentioned above. However, learned Sessions Judge, Narsingdi found the rest two accused not guilty for the offence charged and acquitted them therefrom. 

 10. Mr. Raziur Rahman Chowdhury, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant placed before us First Information Report, charge sheet, confessional statement of accused-appellant made under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the subsequent retraction of the same, post mortem report, evidence on record, impugned judgment and other connected papers as available in the paper book and submits that this is a case of no evidence against appellant. Mr. Raziur Rahman Chowdhury submits that the name of the accused appellant was not mentioned in the First Information Report nor he had any land dispute with informant party and he is absolutely innocent. He further submits that the sole basis of conviction was the confessional statement made by accused-appellant under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but learned Sessions Judge failed to consider that the said confessional statement was obtained by physical torture and inducement by police, which will be evidenced from the prayer for retraction dated 30.11.95 of the same made by appellant and the same was thus not voluntary and true. Citing some decisions he submits that retracted confessional statement cannot be the sole basis of conviction. He further submits that this is a case of highly improbable one. Referring a decision in a case of Safar Ali and others Vs. State reported in 36 DLR185 he submits that confession made by a accused after being kept in police custody for 3 days is highly suspicious. In that case the accused who made confessional statement was convicted under section 394 of the Penal Code and was sentenced to 10 year rigorous imprisonment. On appeal the conviction and sentence were set aside by High Court Division on the ground that accused were in Thana for 3 days without any explanation. Learned Advocate of the appellant referred another decision in case of State Vs. Manik Bala (case of death sentence under section 302 of the Penal Code) reported in 41 DLR 435 wherein it has been held that: 

 "(a) It is now well-settled that a statement recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot be admitted as a substantive evidence against the accused persons, it can only be used for the purpose of contradicting or corroborating the maker of the statement. 

 (b) The confessional statement as its maker is supposed to be the best evidence but when a confession is made foundation for conviction, the Court must be satisfied that it is true and voluntary. The truth or falsity of a confessional statement has to be weighed by the case in the light of all the facts and surrounding circumstances of the case. Normally it would not be quite safe as a matter of prudence to base a conviction for murder on the basis of a retracted confession alone when the confession is open to a good of criticism specially when the proof of the factum of murder is itself solely dependent upon a confession. 

 (c) A retracted confession cannot be used to base a conviction for murder unless corroborated by credible independent evidence. Moreover the version of events given in the confessional statement is not only highly improbable but the facts stated therein were not corroborated by any other evidence and as such it will be unsafe to base a conviction for murder on such a confessional statement. A retracted confession is always open to suspicion and cannot be acted upon unless it is corroborated by credible independent evidence. 

 12. Mr. Raziur Rahman Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the appellant submits that in the instant case the conviction and sentence was based solely on the retracted confessional statement of the accused-appellant which was also not true and voluntary and there was not a single witness, not to speak of credible independent witnesses who corroborated the evidence of confession which is a must according to the decisions referred to above. He further submits that the language of the confessional statement recorded by the Magistrate was in violation of section 364 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and as such it cannot be accepted. He lastly pointed out that from the postmortem report it appears that there were three sharp cutting wounds on the posterior right aspect of the neck but in the First Information Report only one cut wounds on the neck of the deceased was mentioned and on this score also the conviction is not sustainable in law and hence the appeal should be allowed. 

 16. In the wake of rival submissions advanced, the soundness of the same may be considered in the light of evidences led in the case. 

 18. P.W. 2 Abdul Hashem a permanent worker in the mill and uncle of the deceased stated in his evidence that his nephew Joynal was murdered on 4.9.95 at night. His son gave Badli' to him in the Mill on that date. He met with Joynal in the evening and paid Tk. 2/- to Joynal when asked for. He was supposed to go to the Mill. He then stated about return of his brother at 3.00 A.M. and enquired about Joynal and when not found him he along with members of the house including himself searched Joynal in the night. On the following day at 7-30 A.M. he went to the house of Habibur Rahman and told him about missing of Joynal who asked him to search Joynal. On their way back came to know about the recovery of the dead body of Joynal on the drain of Water Development Board near the pump. He suspected accused Quaium, Hafizuddin and Abdul Karim to be the murderer of his nephew. In cross-examination he said that he and his nephew Rahim went to the house of Commissioner. He got the news of recovery of the dead body of his nephew Joynal, went there and then went to police station accompanied by his nephew Bachchu which was about 10/10-30 A.M. He told the police about the incident and brought them near the dead body of the deceased. Police sent the dead body to morgue for post mortem examination. In the evening he had discussion with his brother Hamid. Commissioner Habibur Rahman came to the place of occurrence when the police were making inquest report of the dead body of the deceased. Overtime starts in the Mill after 10.00 P.M. His son was working in M. the Mill for last 3 years as badli worker. He denied that he did not mention the name of accused Qaium to police and that Qaiyum was not a suspect. He denied the defence suggestion that having failed to get the land they have filed the instant false case on the murder of Joynal. 

 27. P.W. 12 S.I. A.K. Barua the then Inspector of Detective Branch, Narsingdi who investigated the case as per order of the Superintendent of Police. He visited the place of occurrence, prepared the sketch map with separate index, recorded the statement of the witnesses, arrested the suspect accused Qaium and he alone admitted the guilt as such his statement was recorded by the Magistrate. On investigation prima facie case was made out against accused Abdul Barek, Hafizuddin and Qaium under section 302/34 of the Penal Code and submitted memo of evidence. But as he was transferred the next Investigating Officer Sub-Inspector Anowar Hossain submitted the charge-sheet. He proved the sketch map Ext. 5, index Ext. 6 and his signature thereto as Ext. 5/1 and 6/1 respectively. In cross-examination he said in the First Information Report place of occurrence was mentioned as Chowala inside the boundary wall of Water Development Board its south eastern corner. He went to the place of occurrence on 6.9.95 and visited the place of occurrence as shown by previous Investigating Officer and the informant. In the First Information Report accused Qaium was not a suspected accused. He arrested accused Qaium on 12.11.95 and forwarded him to Court on 13.11.95 and took him on 3 days remand. He denied that taking on remand the accused was tortured. He denied that he forced accused Qaium to confess implicating accused Barek and Hafiz. He denied that he was influenced by the informant, obtained the confessional statement of accused Qaium by torture and implicated the accused persons falsely. He did not know whether accused Qaium on 30.11.95 through Jailor applied to the Magistrate for retraction of the confessional statement which was forwarded by the Superintendent of Jail on 2.12.95 and seen by the Magistrate on 29.6.96. Witness Hashim did not said about suspicion of accused Qaium. He denied the defence suggestion that he did not investigate the case properly, submitted a perfunctory charge-sheet being illegally gained over by the informant party and deposed falsely. 

 29. P.W.14 Sub-Inspector Anwar Hossain the final Investigating Officer said that he took over the investigation of the case on 27.4.96. He examined the investigation work conducted by previous Investigating Officer A.K. Barua and on receipt of the opinion of the Superintendent of Police on the memo of evidence he filed the charge-sheet against accused Qaium, Abdul Barek and Hafizuddin under section 302/34 of the Penal Code having found prima facie case against them. In cross-examination he said that he did not investigate the case afresh. He denied that he did not perform his duty properly. He said (as asked by the accused) that he did not seize any alamat and that there was no such mention in the charge sheet nor in the case diary. He said that in the Inquest Report it was stated that the wearing apparels like ganji and full pant were pulled out and the dead body was examined but no other injury was found. The said ganji and full pant as mentioned in the inquest report were not seized and no proof of seizure was found during investigation. He failed to give any account that after post mortem examination where and to whom the dead body was handed over. No blood stained earth was seized from the place of occurrence. There was no explanation about this. 

 31. This is all about the evidence on record. 

 32. It transpires from the evidence of P.Ws. mentioned herein above that there is no eye witness of the murder. From the First Information Report it appears that the informant had enmity over land dispute with the accused persons named in the First Information Report but name of the accused-appellant does not appear. There is contradiction about the time of lodging of the First Information Report among P.Ws. 1, 3 and 4. 

 33. It appears that P.Ws. 1-4 who deposed in the case in support of the prosecution case are close relations. Among those 4 P.Ws. two of them, that is also the father and mother of the deceased did neither suspect nor mention the name of the accused appellant, even not in Court. It is only P.W.2 the uncle and P.W.4 the brother who mentioned the name of the accused-appellant. P.W.5 a co-villager does not know anything about the murder. P.W.6 is the First Investigating Officer who prepared the inquest report of the dead body of the deceased and sent the body to the morgue. In cross-examination he said that the First Information Report was lodged at 10-05 A.M. on 5.9.95. P.W. 7 the Doctor who conducted the post mortem examination said about his examination of the dead body and his opinion which was ante mortem and homicidal in nature. P.Ws. 8, 9 and 15 were the witnesses of inquest report. P.W. 10 the then local Municipal Commissioner Habibur Rahman who was declared hostile by the prosecution and cross-examined. In cross-examination he said that on 5.9.95 at 8-00 P.M. the informant went to his house and thereafter lodged the First Information Report at night. P.W.11 the Magistrate who recorded the confessional statement of the accused-appellant under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure claimed to have complied with all the necessary formalities as required by law in recording the statement which was true and voluntary. P.W. 12 Inspector A.K. Barua the 2nd Investigating Officer who conducted the investigation of the ease arrested the accused-appellant on 12.11.95, took the accused-appellant on police remand for 3 days and recorded the confessional statement before the Magistrate and thereafter submitted the memo of evidence to the Superintendent of Police, Narsingdi. P.W. 13 the Police Constable who carried the dead body to morgue. P.W. 14 S.I. Anwar Hossain the final Investigating Officer who did not investigate the case afresh but submitted the charge-sheet on receipt of the opinion from the Superintendent of Police, Narsingdi. 

 "In the instant case accused Qaium made confessional statement implicating accused Hafizuddin and Barek but except the said statement there is no other independent evidence against the said 2 accuseds, so there is no any independent corroboration except the said confessional statement accused Hafizuddin and Barek cannot be held guilty for murdering deceased Joynal." 

 35. On critical analysis of the evidence on record it appears that in the instant case there were no corroboration of the confessional statement made by the accused-appellant, no circumstantial evidence leading to prove the guilt of the accused-appellant. The learned Sessions Judge solely relying upon the confessional statement believing it to be true and voluntary based his order of conviction and sentence. 

 37. From the decisions referred by the learned Advocate for the appellant it has been consistently held that confession made by an accused after being kept in police custody for 3 days, such a confession is highly suspicious. Confessional statement cannot be admitted as a substantive evidence against accused persons. It is also not safe to base a conviction for murder on the basis of retracted confession and that a retracted confession cannot be used to base a conviction for murder unless corroborated by credible independent evidence. Confessing accused kept 2 days in police custody preceding his production before Magistrate for recording confessional statement such a statement must be taken with a grain of salt. 

 40. It has also been observed by our Appellate Division that where there is no other evidence to show affirmatively that any portion of the exculpatory element in the confession is false, the Court must accept or reject the confession as a whole and cannot accept only the inculpatory element rejecting the exculpatory element as inherently incredible. In the instant case the learned Sessions Judge based on the inculpatory portion of the confession made by the accused appellant and awarded the punishment and disbelieved the exculpatory part of the confession having no other independent evidence ignoring the fact that there is no corroborative evidence of the inculpatory statement of the confession. It appears that the learned Sessions Judge misconstrued the meaning of section 34 of the Penal Code. In the absence of proof of prior planning of common intention there cannot be any act said to be acts done by in furtherance of the common intention. 

 41. From the above citations as well as from the facts and circumstances of the case it is found that preceding to make the confession the accused-appellant was in police custody and there was no corroborative evidence to the said confession. Suspicion however strong cannot take the place of proof. It is true that in a criminal trial the question of motive is of very little importance when there is direct and reliable evidence to prove the crime. But in the present case there is no direct or reliable evidence to proved the crime so motive became a vital element but no such motive was found in the instant case. Admittedly there was no dispute between the informant and the accused-appellant. In this case admittedly there is no eye witness nor any witness to connect the accused-appellant in the murder of deceased Joynal save and except his confessional statement Ext. 4. 

 42. The possibility of the accused being influenced by threat or otherwise from the police cannot altogether be eliminated. In view of the matter we are not inclined to accept the confession made as true and voluntary. There is absolutely no iota of evidence corroborating the confessional statement either. So the conviction of the accused-appellant on the basis of such confessional statement without any corroboration could not be legally sustained.
